SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, arrear is a function of many factors. 
Arrears is a function of how much cu rrent demand you raise in the current 
assessment year. The moment a current demand is raised, it becomes an arrear, if 
it is not paid. 
Secondly, arrear is also a function of the amount of litigation. If a matter goes 
up in appeal to the High Court or the Supreme Court and there is an interim order 
of stay, then, the amount not collected becomes arrears. So, you cannot put your 
finger and say that arrears gone up because of this, or arrears have gone down 
because of this. 
Thirdly, if the total estimated income  from a particular tax increases, say, 
by about 20-25 per cent a year, as shown in the Budget, then, it is fair to expect that 
the arrears also will increase because to that extent demands has been raised for that 
tax. So, I do not think these are amenable to very easy categorizations and easy 
answers. All I can tell you is, in the period April-October, 2005.I believe, we have 
collected about Rs. 3,660 crores of arrears. And I am hopeful that we will collect 
as much this year as we did last year which, as you know, was a record 
collection year for arrears.

SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, I think this a very good question reflecting, 
obviously, the vast experience of Dr. Malaisamy. You cannot expect the same 
growth rate year after year after year. You are right. You are absolutely right and I 
compliment you for that. But the untapped potential in income tax is still very 
large. Unless we bring more people into the tax net, you cannot expect this 
growth rate. I think, by and large, in corporate tax we have a fair idea of the 
potential assessee base. For income-tax, I think, the assessee's base is grossly 
under-estimated. There are many, many more people, you know them, I know 
them, we all know them, who ought to by paying tax, who don't pay tax. This is 
why we are now concentrating on-using information and intelligence to zero in on 
people who ought to be paying tax, but don't pay any tax at all. And the people 
who ought to be paying more tax are paying less tax. The Annual Information 
Report is meant to identify such people through their expenditure habits. The 
banking cash transaction tax is meant to identify such people from the large cash 
withdrawals that they do. I am confident that as the base increases, the growth 
rate will remain reasonably high. But if the base is not increased, I entirely agree 
with the hon. Member, this growth rate cannot be sustained year after year. 
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Sir, I would like to know from the hon. Minister 
why the rate of increase in  the collection of central excise is much less than 
that of other direct taxes. It is just 1 /4th of the direct taxes and only 1/3rd of the 
central customs. Are there any special reasons why the buoyancy is not 
reflected in the collection of central excise? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, Yes, the central excise is not reflecting the 
same buoyancy as other direct taxes. The reasons are following. Firstly, non-POL 
capital goods imports and non-POL non-capital goods imports are growing at a 
very fast rate this year, which means the CVD that is collected on imported 
goods is offset against the central excise duty paid. It is only when those goods 
produce other goods which are exciseable that the excise revenues will come. 
There is always a lead and lag in that. The offsetting takes place first an revenues 
come later. So, CVD is being offset against the central excise paid. 
Secondly, exports are growing at a brisk pace this year. My recollection is, 
exports are growing by about 22-23 per cent. Sir, in all exported goods, the entire 
excise duty is rebated as drawback. It is the high imports of non-POL goods 
and the high growth of exports which is affecting the growth

Subsidy on kerosene 
*83.  SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA:† 
SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Oil Marketing Companies subsidized PDS 
kerosene by about Rs. 12 per litre and combined with subsidies on domestic LPG, 
the expenditure was about Rs. 18000 crore in 2004-2005; 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Vijay J. Darda. 
9 

RAJYA  SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
(b) if so, whether this subsidized PDS kerosene was given to only targeted 
consumers or there was siphoning of this commodity to non-household users; 
and 
(c) in what manner the Oil Marketing Companies propose to subsidize as the 
kerosene demand is expected to increase by one percent annually and what is the 
estimated amount of subsidy every year? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) During the year 2004-05, the public sector oil companies have 
absorbed under-recoveries of the order of Rs. 7.96/litre on the sale of PDS 
kerosene. In addition, the Government provided for subsidy of 
Rs. 0.82/litre from the fiscal budget. 
At the time of announcement of the dismantling of Administered Pricing 
Mechanism (APM) effective 1st April,  2002, it was announced that the 
Government subsidy on PDS kerosene would be on a flat rate basis and provided 
from the fiscal budget. It was also announced that after providing for the 
Government subsidy, retail prices were to vary as per changes in international 
prices. 
But notwithstanding the steep rise in international prices of SKO & PLG, 
oil marketing companies (OMCs) have not been able to revise the price of PDS 
kerosene since April 2002 and that of domestic LPG since November 2004. In 
consequence, they have suffered under-recoveries to the tune of Rs. 17,842 crore 
on sale of these products during the year 2004-05. 
(b) and (c) With a view to assessing the genuine demand for kerosene 
in different States/UTs, the Government commissioned a comprehensive 
study through the National Council of Applied Research (NCAER) in 
December, 2004. NCAER have submitted their report in October, 2005. 
The study estimates siphoning off of kerosene from PDS to non-household 
use as 18.1 per cent of the total sale of PDS kerosene in the country. The 
report also inter alia recommends that taking out APL card holders from 
the purview of subsidies would amount to savings of 41.2% on the current 
kerosene subsidy. 
10 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In order to check the black marketing of Public Distribution System (PDS) 
kerosene, the Central Government have made provision in the Kerosene 
(Restriction on Use and Fixation of Ceiling Price) Order, 1993, issued under the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955, that dealers cannot sell PDS kerosene at a 
price higher than the price fixed by the Government or Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) and that the PDS kerosene dealers should prominently display stock-
cum-price board at the place of business including the pl ace of store on 
conspicuous place. State Governments undertake the distribution of PDS 
kerosene through their PDS network. It is also their duty to implement the 
Control Orders issued by the Central Government under the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955. 
With a view to strengthening the kerosene distribution system so that PDS 
kerosene is made available to the consumers at the right price and diversion is 
checked, the Government have also launched the "Jan Kerosene Pariyojana" as a 
pilot project in 420 blocks in the country effective 2nd October, 2005. The 
project involves strengthening the system of transporting kerosene from 
OMC depots to PDS fair price shops, the distribution infrastructure at the 
block and sub-block levels, and the involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
and Gram Sabhas in monitoring the distribution of PDS kerosene. 
During 2005-06, through the fiscal budget, Government have provided Rs. 
3,600 crore as subsidies on PDS kerosene and deomestic LPG.

Insurance of farmers 
*85. SHRI R.K. ANAND: Will the Mini ster of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Agriculture Insurance Company of India Ltd. 
has, since its inception, insured 18 million farmers; and 
(b) if so, whether the Varsha Bima Scheme is not getting any support from 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) and (b) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
(a)The Agriculture Insurance Company of India Ltd. (AICL) has reported that 
since its inception in December 2002, it has insured 2,86,11,127 farmers, 
upto Rabi 2004-05 under the National Agricutural Insurance Scheme (NAIS). 
It has insured 1,25,453 farmers during Kharif 2005 under the Varsha Bima 
Scheme. 
(b) AICL, has launched the Varsha Bima Scheme purely as an insurance  product 
without Government subsidy. 
SHRI R.K. ANAND: Mr. Chairman, Sir, in reply to my question the hon. 
Minister has given the precise number of farmers who are insured. What is the 
percentage of farmers in the whole of India who are covered by this scheme? 
What steps are being taken to creat e awareness about this echeme among 
other farmers? 
SHRI R CHIDAMBARAM: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the estimated number of 
farmer families in this country is approximately ten crores. Approximately, at the 
end of last year, 4.67 crores had access to any kind of institutional credit So, we 
are talking about a very small proportion of farmers who are covered under 
insurance. This scheme, which is now being implemented by the NAIS, is 
mandatory for all farmers who availed of a crop loan from a bank. It is optional for 
non-loanee farmers. As bank credit increases, as more and more farmers access 
institutional credit from public sector banks, the number of farmers who are 
covered under this scheme will increase. But for non-loanee farmers, of course, 
this scheme is optional. Non-loanee farmers cannot be compelled to take 
insurance. The other scheme, which has been introduced recently, that is, the 
Varsha Bima Scheme, is a pure insurance scheme with no element of subsidy 
in it. That scheme has attracted a sizeable number of people. But I admit that 
the numbers are not very large. The numbers are expected to grow. But it is a pure 
insurance scheme. In the absence of subsidy, many farmers may not think it 
advantageous to them to come under the scheme. 
SHRI R.K. ANAND: Is there any proposal to cover apple crop which is 
spoiled by hailtorms, which is a common phenomenon in Himachal Pradesh? 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, at the moment, the NAIS covers paddy, 
wheat, jowar, bajra, maize, ragi, kora, kodokuki, green gram, black gram, red 
gram, horse gram, oil seeds, sugarcane, cotton and potato. Whether it should be 
extended to the horticultural crops, it is a matter that can be considered.

SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is acute shortage of LPG cylinders in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that undertakings like Indian Oil and Hindustan 
Petroleum have directed its LPG dealers to stop allotting new LPG connections; 
and 
(d) if so, what steps have been taken by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKARAIYAR): (a) to (d) Astatement is laid on the Table of the House. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the house by Shri Tariq 
Anwar. 
24 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Demand for LPG in the country is met by a combination of 
domestic production and imports. A temporary shortage of LPG emerged in 
September 2005  when Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL), the single largest domestic 
supplier of LPG, announced a shut down of their Fluidized Catalytic Cracker 
(FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work with effect from October 2005, at 
just about the time goal LPG supplies became tight, domestic production was 
affected by the fire at Mumbai High and partly on account of the impact of 
Hurricane Katrina on US refineries. This upset the plans made by our Oil 
Marketing Companies (OMCs) to effect imports in time to offset the anticipated 
shortage in supplies on account of the RIL shut down. 
Further rumours in the market that OMCs would not be able to meet the 
demand led to a sudden spurt in demand. There were also a strike in bo ttling 
plants in the National Capital Territory (NCT) area towards the end of 
September 2005 which aggravated the situation. The Ministry took matters in 
hand early in October, 2005 when it was decided that through a combination 
of inventory management and imports, directly handled by a composite task 
force of the OMCs under the close supervision of the Government, physical 
shortage of supply would be overcome as quickly as possible. It was also 
decided that bottling plants in the NCT area would work on Sunday, 9th 
October 2005 and other holidays. On the basis of these decisions, it was 
announced that they physical shortage in the NCT area would end by 
Dusshera and substantively in the rest  of the country by Deepavali. These 
objectives have been largely achieved. In addition to the arrangements made 
earlier by OMCs to import 642 Thousand Metric Tonnes (TMT) of LPG 
during the period October-December 2005, arrangements have been made to 
import an additional quantity of 237.9 TMT during this period, 116 TMT of which 
has already reached the country. Thus, the overall physical shortage in the country 
at present has been reduced to only about 1.5% of the average monthly 
consumption of LPG. However, the backlog at the micro-level may very from 
market to market on account of operational reasons. The situation is expected to 
normalize further by the end of November, 2005 on the restoration of 
production in RIL's refinery. Moreover, while OMCs are striving to ensure 
supplies to distributors in accordance with the registered customer strength of 
the distributor, the active cooperation of State Governments is required to cap, 
reduce and eventually eliminate 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
the diversion of domestic LPG to the black market and unauthorized use which 
takes place on account of the wide gap between the retail price of LPG for 
domestic use and the market price for commercial LPG. The Union 
Government in the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas has alerted State 
Governments to the imperative need to curtail diversion and other malpractices 
by enforcing the control orders issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 
1955. OMCs have also been directed to ensure adherence to Marketing 
Discipline Guidelines, 2001. 
In view of the temporary LPG shortage, OMCs had restricted the release of new 
connections effective September 2005 but, in view of the improvement in the 
situation, they have accepted the Ministry's request to resume the release of new 
connections from 1st December, 2005.

Plan to control floods 
†*88. SHRI UDAY PR ATAP SINGH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any comprehensive plan has been made by Government for 
controlling floods in the flood-affected areas during monsoon; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MONAN DEV): (a) and (b) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Flood throughout the world cannot be fully controlled. It is to be managed to best 
of ability on technical merit of the pr oblem from place to place. However, 
flood Management being within the purview of States, the schemes for flood control 
are planned, funded and exectuted by the State Governments. The role of 
Central Government is technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. UPA 
Government gave special emphasis on this issue in the National Common 
Minimum Programme. 
Central Government, however, has also been initiating various measures for 
assisting the States in the management of floods. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog, set up 
by the Government of India in 1976 to look into flood problem and suggest 
remedial measures, submitted its report in 1980. The recommendations of the 
Rashtriya Barh Ayog which formed the framework for flood management strategy 
in the country were forwarded to the various State Governments for 
implementation. Several other expert committees were also constituted by the 
Government from time to time to study the problem relating to flood and its 
management, the recommendations of which were also sent to the respective 
State Governments for implementation. Ganga Flood Control Commission for 
Ganga Basin States constituted in 1972 prepared Comprehensive Plans for Flood 
Management for all the 23 river systems of Ganga. Likewise, Brahmaputra Board 
which started functioning at Guwahati in 1982 prepared Master Plans for Flood 
Management for Brahmaputra, Barak and its major tributaries. These plans were 
forwarded to concerned State Governments for implementation. 
The National Water Policy 2002 has recommended for preparation of basin 
wise Master Plan for flood control and management providing therein 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
adequate flood cusion in reservoir projects, giving overriding consideration of 
flood control in reservoir regulation policy. It has further emphasised on non-
structural measures like regulation of settlements and economic activities in 
flood plains as well as modernizati on and expansion of flood forecasting 
activities. 
In order to mitigate the damages from floods, a nationwide flood 
forecasting and warning system, as a non-structural measure, has been 
established by the Central Water Commission which issues flood forecasts at 173 
stations in the country of which 145 stations are for river stage forecast and 28 
for inflow forecast. The Flood Forecasting Network is being upgraded in the current 
plan by way of installation of modern data collection/ data communication system 
to enable collection and transmission of real time data to forecast formulation 
centres and dissemination of the forecasts to user agencies for which a scheme 
estimated to cost Rs. 51 crore has already been approved by the Government 
of India. 
During 2004, the Government of India has constituted a Task Force for Flood 
Management/Erosion Control under the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central 
Water Commission with representatives of State Governments, various Central 
Ministries and experts as members to examine the problem of flood and erosion in 
Assam and neighbouring States, West Bengal, Bihar and Eastern Uttar 
Pradesh. The Task Force has inter alia recommended taking up of reservoir 
projects as permanent/ long term measures for flood management. 
The Government of India have been taking effective steps in this direction. An 
agreement was reached with Nepal for survey and investigation and preparation 
of Detailed Project Report for Sapta Kosi High Dam Multipurpose Project and Sun 
Kosi Storage Cum Diversion Scheme for which a Joint Project Office has 
already been opened in Nepal in August 2004. This project has flood control 
as one of the major benefits. Nepal has also agreed for undertaking the joint 
feasibility study of Kamla and preliminary study of Bagmati Multipurpose 
Project to ascertain likely constraints in implementation of these projects so that 
the same could be appropriately addressed. The Government of India had also 
approved implementation of Pagladiya Multipurpose Project in Assam in 2001 at 
a cost of Rs. 542.90 crore (Revised tentative cost Rs. 1069.40 crore) which has 
flood control as a major benefit. In addition to the above, the Government of 
India has 
30 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
also been providing Central assistance to the State Governments to take up 
critical anti erosion/flood management works. A scheme amounting to Rs. 195.63 
crore (central share) was approved during the 10th Plan for Ganga Basin States. 
Similarly a scheme of Rs. 150 crore has been approved for North Eastern Region 
including Sikkim and North Bengal. Brahmaputra Board has also executed anti 
erosion works worth Rs. 21.91 crore. Another scheme amounting to Rs. 41.28 crore 
has been approved to be fully funded by the Government of India for the protection 
of Majuli Island. Governments of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are being provided 
financial assistance for maintenance of Gandak and Kosi embankments (Nepal 
portion), which they execute after every flood season. Assistance is also being 
rendered to Bihar for the scheme namely, "Extension, raising and strengthening 
of embankments for rivers Lalbakeya, Kamla, Bagmati and Khando".

Declining expenditure on social and infrastructure development 
*92. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that various State Governments are unable to spend 
much on social and infrastructure development of their respective state as they 
are facing acute financial crisis due to heavy loan amount and 
mismanagement of financial structures; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government are considering any structured and transparent    approach to 
lesion the burden of debt on various states so that they can increase their expenditure 
and investments on infrastructure and social sector; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (e) It is a 
fact that various State Governments have been spending less on the 
36 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
social sector and physical infrastructure as evidenced by low ratio of such 
expenditure to their gross State Do mestic Product. Increasing non 
developmental expenditure in the total expenditure of the States has led to partial 
crowding out of the expenditure in social sector and infrastructure. For many 
States, three major committed expenditure  viz., interest payments, salaries 
and pensions equalled almost their entire revenue receipts, leaving very little 
fiscal space for sustained expenditure on social and infrastructure development. 
In order to reduce the interest burden of the States, Government of India 
operated a debt swap scheme in recent years. Swapping of Gol loans with interest 
rates of 13 per cent and above has helped the States to reduce their debt 
servicing costs to a considerable level. 
Higher resource transfers under devolution of States' share in Central taxes 
and duties, social sector specific grants for States whose per capita expenditure on 
Education and Health are below the group average and gap filling non plan 
revenue deficit grants recommended by the Twelfth Finance Commisson (TFC) 
are expected to supplement the resources of States to increase the quality of 
expenditure and investment in priority sectors. 
Government of India has also increased its support under Central sector and 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes to the States for filling critical gaps in social sector 
including health, education and nutrition. Budgetary support has been enhanced to 
Sarva Shikska Abhiyan, Integrated Child Development Scheme, Mid-day meal 
scheme. National Rural Health Mission has been launched this year. 
Government of India has accepted the recommendation of the TFC for a Debt 
Consolidation and Relief Facility that would enable the States to pay lesser 
amount of repayment of principal and interest. 
In addition, a debt waiver scheme, also recommended by TFC, linked to 
reduction of revenue deficit of States, has also been put in place. This should 
help the States in reducing their debt burden. 
Reduction and subsequent elimination of revenue deficit by 2008-09 should 
provide the much needed fiscal space and unlock the resources for higher 
investment in social sector and physical infrastructure.

Rate of interest on home loans 
*95. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India proposes to increase the rate of interest 
on home loans; 
(b) if so, since when it is proposed to be increased; 
(c) the extent to which it shall have an  adverse effect on the persons who 
have taken such loans; and 
(d) steps to be taken by Government to protect the common man from the 
builders? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (d) 
Interest rates on advances above Rs. 2 lakh have been deregulated. These interest 
rates are determined by the banks themselves with the approval of their Boards. 
In order to enhance transparency in bank's pricing of the loan products, banks 
have been advised to fix their Benchmark Prime Lending Rate (BPLR) after 
taking into account considerations such as actual cost of funds, operating 
expenses, minimum margin to cover regulatory requirement of 
provisioning/capital charge and profit margin. Accordingly, banks are now fixing 
interest rates to be charged to a particular borrower subject to BPLR and spread 
guidelines. However, banks are free to charge interest on housing loans without 
reference to their BPLR. Therefore, the rate of interest on housing loans may be 
below or above the BPLR. Banks also have freedom to offer loans on floating 
rates by using market benchmarks in a transparent manner.

Recommendations of Paul Committee 
581. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the K. Roy Paul Committee, set up to suggest 
ways to tackle the worsening congestion of flights over Delhi and Mumbai 
airports, has submitted its report; 
(b) if so, the details of the major recommendations made or the action plan 
suggested by the Committee; and 
(c) the short/long term plans drawn up to decongest the skies at both the 
airports and their present status? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Committee has made recommendations to decongest the air traffic 
and enhance the air traffic capacity at Delhi and Mumbai, in particular, 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
and some other airports f the country. These recommendations based on short, 
medium and long term measures range from improving ground infrastructure 
facilities, technological improvements in Communication, Navigation, 
Surveillance (CNS) and Air Traffic Management (ATM), Airspace management, 
Maintenance procedures of airside, organisational structure of CNS-ATM 
services, separation of Helicopter and General Aviation Services particularly 
during peak hours, Manpower Planning, recruitment policy, training and skill 
development etc. 
(c) The short/long term plans inter-alia include: establishment of 
Clearance Delivery Position to enable pilots to expedite departures; 
introduction of Auto Release procedures to release the departures on standard 
routes upto a certain height for expeditious departures; deployment of additional 
manpower; creating separate helipads and corridors for helicopters; 
construction of new high speed exit and parallel taxiways to reduce the runway 
occupancy time and enable operations from both the runways; restructuring of 
airspace; filling up of vacant posts in ATC; upgradation of Air Traffic Control 
Automation system and installation of Advanced Surface Movement Guidance 
& Control System; introduction of Air Traffic Flow Management System to enable 
the departures from airports other than Delhi and Mumbai.

Norms of Passenger Aircraft Cockpit Door 
587. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Dire ctorate General of Civil Aviation has 
revised the norms for making the passenger aircraft cockpit doors 
bulletproof; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
51 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details of the revised norms and how the revised norms are 
different from the existing ones; and 
(c) whether the DGCA has recommended any new norms for security 
training course to crew members? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) and (b) Both the old & new norms require 
installation of bullet proof door which is capable of being locked and unlocked from 
cockpit by. any pilot. However, under the old norms the cockpit door was to be 
bullet proofed for only those aeroplanes engaged in scheduled air transport 
services (Passenger) or cargo operations where provision is available to carry 
passengers irrespective of the All up weight or passenger carrying capacity. 
However, as per the revised norms both scheduled and non scheduled passengers 
carrying aeroplanes of a maximum of certified take off mass in exess of 45,500 
Kg. or with a passenger seating capacity greater that 60 shall be equipped with an 
approved flight by small arms fire and grenade shrapnel, and to resist forcible 
intrusion of unauthorized persons. The new norms thus differ in the extent of 
their applicability and also on the need for provision of monitoring system in 
the cockpit for monitoring the entire door area outside the flight crew 
compartment. 
(c) The requirement for taining crew  members on security aspects is 
already provided in the existing instructions.

589. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the short-term measures proposed by Government to reduce delays due to 
lack of take-off and landing space at major airports like Delhi; 
(b) whether Government are aware that on average the planes circle over 
Delhi for 30 minutes to one hour just to land or take-off; 
(c) what short-term steps have been put in place to reduce such delays since 
November 1,2005; 
(d) whether it is a fact that lack of software or technical expertise of our air 
traffic controllers is creating further problems; and 
(e) the steps proposed to immediately improve take-off and landing times 
of our planes and reduce delays? 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) Various m easures have been introduced by 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) to reduce delays in take off and landing of 
flights at major airports such as establishment of Clearance Delivery Position to 
enable pilots to expedite departures, introduction of Auto Release procedures 
to release the departures on standard routes upto a certain height for expeditious 
departures, starting the construction of new high speed exit and parallel taxiways to 
reduce the runway occupancy time and enable operations from both the runways, 
and initiating the upgradation of Air Traffic Control Automation System and 
installation of Advanced Surface Movement Guidance & Control System at Delhi 
and Mumbai airports. Besides, in order to reduce congestion in air for timely

World Development Report, 2006 
†622. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: W ill the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that in the World Development Report 2006, 
World Bank has mentioned that bribe and price rise are the worst secret tax for 
poor people, if so, whether people of India also suffer from it; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
92 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) what steps are being taken by Government to make people free from it; 
(c) whether he will consider upon the recommendations of the World Bank 
in future; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. The World Development Report, 
2006, while suggesting certain general basic principles for mobilizing tax revenues in 
ways that minimize efficiency costs and at the same time do not undermine 
equity, states, "In many instances, the most important taxes affecting the poor 
are not formal ones levied through the tax code, but implicit taxes, including 
bribes and inflation". However, the statement has been made in general and there 
is no particular reference to India. 
(b) In order to reduce the scope of un accounted economy, Government has 
taken several measures such as significant reduction and rationalisation of duties and 
taxes, delicensing and deregulation of industries and essential economic services and 
emphasis on good governance in both public and private sectors. In addition, to the 
above measures, specific anti-inflationary measures of the Government include 
effective supply and demand management of essential commodities through 
liberal trade and tariff policies and strengthening of the Public Distribution 
System. 
(c) and (d) The recommendations of the multilateral organisations are kept in 
view by the Government while formulating appropriate economic policies.

Third Round Table of Ministers in-charge of Panchayati Raj-Raipur, 23-24 
September 2004 
Ministers in-charge of Panchayati Raj, and their representatives, bearing in mind 
the spirit of cooperative federalism which must inform the effective 
implementation of Panchayati Raj as set out in Part IX of the Constitution of 
India and related provisions, agreed to recommend to their respective 
Governments, for joint acceptance by the Centre and the States, the following 
points of action: 
II.  Reservations for Women 
(i) It is clear that women have been able to enlarge their representation 
beyond the minimum 33V 1/3% prescribed by the Constitution. In 
Karnataka, 45% of the elected offices are occupied by women and in 
Uttar Pradesn, 54% of the Zilla Pa nchayats Presidents are women.

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) In promoting larger social objectives through PRIs, States may be 
sensitized to issues of gender em powerment so that the unintended 
consequences of such policies is not to diminish the role of women in 
Panchayati Raj. 
(iii) The Constitution does provide for the rotation of seats reserved for 
women but does not prescribe the number of terms for which seats may 
be reserved before rotation. Seats may be reserved for one term or two 
terms or more depending upon the provisions made by the State 
Legislature in the State law. There are different practices being adopted 
in the different States and there are different practices under 
contemplation in several States. This being so, the option to reserve 
seats for more than one-term is open but it is for the State legislature 
to decide the number of terms for which seats will remain reserved. 
(iv) The empowerment of women through reservations in the panchayats 
is a necessary first step but needs to be reinforced by a number of 
other measures such as: 
(a) the provision of Women Component Plans in the budgets of the 
PRIs; 
(b) linkages with Self Help Groups (SHGs); 
(c) adequate training and capacity building; 
(d) encouragement to political parties to put up women 
candidates;

elected to posts in the PR system;

priorities being raised in meetin gs of Gram Sabhas and Ward 
Sabhas (or equivalent sub-Gram Sabha forums);

sub-Gram Sabha forums.

682. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Anti-Adulteration Cell for petroleum products has 
been wound up in 2004; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefore; 
(c) what alternative steps have been  taken to check adulteration in 
petroleum products; 
(d) whether the alternative steps have proved more eff ective to checking 
adulteration in petroleum products; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) Yes,Sir. The Anti-Adulteration Cell (AAC), 
was set up in March 2001 under the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas 
(MOP&NG). It was found to be ineffective in its functioning on account of the 
possible involvement of some of its officers who are under investigation by the 
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for undesirable activities. Therefore, a 
one-man committee under the chairmanship of Additional Secretary, Ministry 
of Petroleum & Natural Gas was set up in April, 2004 to conduct an extensive 
review of the working of the AAC. The report showed that the AAC, with its 
existing structure and functions, could not 
144 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
play a meaningful role in the Ministry's efforts to curb the menace of 
adulteration. Accordingly, the Cell was wound up in July 2004. 
(c) to (e) The Government/Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) have taken the following steps to contain the menace of 
adujteration: 
(i)    Under the Control Orders issued by the Government to prevent fuel 
adulteration, under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, State 
Governments are empowered to take action against those indulging in 
adulteration. Government have taken up this matter with all the State 
Governments/Union Territory Administrations to step up 
inspections/surprises checks to ensure that adulteration-related 
activities are minimized and to exercise vigil/conduct inspections at 
various private firms, factories, processing units, etc., under their 
jurisdictions so as to identify the perpetrators of adulteration and take 
stringent action against them within the available legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail Outlets and 
also take action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) and 
Dealership Agreements against those indulging in adulteration and 
malpractices. MDG provide for penalty of termination of dealership 
in cases of adulteration being established. 
(iii) As advised by the Government, Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have 
created a separate wing to report to  a Director other than Director 
(Marketing), which will oversee and monitor all activities and 
operations to curb adulteration and specify norms and guidelines in 
this regard. 
(iv) Keeping in view the misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the 
import of SKO by private parties has been canalized through 
OMCs. 
(v) OMCs have introduced new tamper proof tank-truck locking systems 
to prevent en route adulteration by transporters. 
(vi) Information Technology (IT) solutions like monitoring movement of tank 
trucks through Global Positioning System (GPS) and monitoring 
level of fuel tank in Retail Outlets through retail automation are 
being introduced. 
145 

RAJYA  SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
(vii) Branding of Retail Outlets and third party certification of Retail 
Outlets have been initiated by the OMCs. 
(viii) Effective 2nd October 2005, Government launched the Jan Kerosene 
Pariyojana as a pilot projects in 420 blocks for a period of six months 
with a view to strengthening and streamlining the infrastructure for 
kerosene distribution and involving the Gram Sabhas and Gram 
Panchayats and State Panchayati Raj Institutions in the supervision 
of PDS kerosene distribution, so as to ensure that entitled 
beneficiaries actually receive their en titlement and diversion to 
adulteration and black-marketing is capped, reversed and eventually 
eliminated. The pilot project is being concurrently evaluated by 
NCAER and, on the basis of the experience gained, Government will 
determine the possibility and desirability of extending the Pariyojana to 
cover all blocks in the country. 
Measures to check adulteration are kept under continuous review of the 
Government.

150 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) whether there is any shortage of domestic LPG in Karnataka; 
(e)whether the new domestic LPG connections have been stopped in 
Karnataka; 
(f) whether Government are aware that nearly 25 per cent of the LPG meant 
for domestic consumption is being di verted to hotels, restaurants and 
automobile filling stations; and 
(g) if so, the steps taken to stop this pilferage? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) At pres ent, Public Sector Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) have 47.82 lakh LPG domestic consumers in the State of 
Karnataka including 17.88 lakh in Bangalore city. 
(c) The average quantity of LPG required in Karnataka is about 49,586 Metric 
Tonne (MT) per month. 
(d) and (e) Demand for LPG in the country is met by a combination of 
domestic production and imports. Atemporary shortage of LPG emerged in 
September 2005 when Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL), the single largest domestic 
supplier of LPG, announced a shut down of their Fluidized Catalytic Cracker 
(FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work with effect from October 2005, at 
just about the time global LPG supplies became tight, domestic production 
was affected by the fire at Mumbai High and partly on account of the impact of 
Hurricane Katrina on US refineries. This upset the plans made by our Oil 
Marketing Companies (OMCs) to effect imports in time to offset the anticipated 
shortage in supplies on account of the RIL shut down.  
In view of this, OMCs have restricted the release of new connections in 
country from September 2005 onward. The situation is expected to normalize

RIL's refinery. In view of improvement in situation, OMCs have decided to 
resume release of new connections from 1st December 2005.

151

measures have been taken to prevent the diversion/black marketing of 
domestic LPG cylinders for commercial purposes:— 
 (i) Under the LPG (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Order, 2000 
promulgated under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 the 
diversion/black marketing of domestic LPG cylinders for 
commercial purposes by the distributors of OMCs is prohibited. The 
State Governments are empowered to take action against erring 
distributors under the provisions of this Order. 
(ii) State Governments are alerted from time to time to crack down the 
diversion of domestic cylinders for unauthorized usage. 
(iii) As per the Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) for LPG 
distributors, in case of establishment of any diversion/black 
marketing of domestic LPG cylinder for commercial purposes, the 
following action is take against the distributor: 
(a) Fine of Rs. 20,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at 
commercial rates for 1 st offence. 
(b) Fine of Rs. 50,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at 
commercial rates for 2nd offence, and 
(c) Termination of the distributorship for 3rd offence. 
(iv) The officials of OMCs carry out random checks at distributor's 
godown, delivery point as well as  enroute to ensure that no 
diversion/black marketing takes place. Action against the erring 
distributor is taken in terms of MDG/or Distributorship 
Agreement.

the bench mark crude oil in the USA) rose from US$ 56.35/ bbl to US$ 62.28/bbl during the

(b) The fluctuation in international oil prices has a cascading effect on the overall 
economy affecting primary sectors such as transport, power, fertilizers etc. besides 
generating inflationary potential and slowing down the growth rate of the economy. 
(c) With a view to containing the burden of the increase in international prices on 
consumers of petroleum products, Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have 
not passed on the full increase in international prices to the domestic consumer prices of 
these products. The burden borne by oil companies will, of course, go up to the extent 
that domestic prices are not revised upwards when international prices shoot up. With 
effect from 1st August 2004 Government had worked out a price band mechanism, 
allowing OMCs freedom to revise the prices of petrol and diesel within the prescribed 
price band. However, the steep and volatile increase in the international prices of crude oil 
resulted in the ceiling of the price band being breached within weeks of its being made 
operational resulting in the mechanism being placed in abeyance. It is hoped that when 
international prices stabilize, or Government so decides, the price band mechanism might 
be restored. It may be noted that private sector companies are free to fix their prices.

698. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND

(a) whether there was shortage of supply of LPG in the Capital and other States of 
the country during September and October, 2005; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the specific reasons for shortage of LPG; 
(d) the measures taken to overcome the shortage of LPG; 
164 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) whether Government are aware of the diversion of domestic LPG cylinders 
for commercial use and in cars; 
(f) if so, the measures taken to check this illegal use of LPG; and 
(g) by when, the supply of LPG is likely to become normal? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRIMANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (d) and (g) Demand for LPG in the country is met by a 
combination of domestic production and imports. A temporary shortage of LPG 
emerged in September 2005 when Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL), the single largest 
domestic supplier of LPG announced a shut down of their Fluidized Catalytic Cracker 
(FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work with effect from October 2005, at just 
about the time global LPG supplies became tight, domestic production was affected by 
the fire at Mumbai High and partly on account of the impact of Hurricane Katrina on 
US refineries. This upset the plans made by our Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) to 
effect imports in time to offset the anticipated shortage in supplies on account of the 
RIL shut down. 
Further rumours in the market that OMCs would not be able to meet the demand 
led to a sudden spurt in demand. There were also a strike in bottling plants in the National 
Capital Territory (NCT) area towards the end of September 2005 which aggravated the 
situation. The Ministry took matters in hand early in October, 2005 when it was decided 
that through a combination of inventory management and imports, directly handled by a 
composite task force of the OMCs under the close supervision of the Government, 
physical shortages of supply would be overcome as quickly as possible. It was also 
decided that bottling plants in the NCT area would work on Sunday, 9th October 2005 
and other holidays. On the basis of these decisions, it was announced that the physical 
shortage in the NCT area would end by Dusshera and substantively in the rest of the 
country by Deepavali. These objectives have been largely achieved. In addition to the 
arrangements made earlier by OMCs to import 642 Thousand Metric Tonnes (TMT) 
of LPG during the period October-December 2005, arrangements have been 
made to import an additional quantity of 237.9 TMT during this period, 116 TMT of 
which has already reached the country. Thus, the overall physical shortage in the country 
at present has been reduced to only about 1.5% of the average monthly consumption of 
LPG However, the backlog at the micro-level may vary from market to market

on account of operational reasons. The situation is expected to normalize further by the end 
of November 2005 on the restoration of production in RIL's refinery.

Black-Marketing of LPG Cylinders 
706. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that consumers across the country suffered in the 
recent past from acute scarcity of LPG refills leading to its black-marketing 
in various parts; 
(b) the reasons for the scarcity, including month-wise details of demand and 
supply since January, 2004; 
(c) the action taken, if any against LPG supply and distribution agencies against 
whom complaints of misappropriation or misuse have been lodged/ detected; 
(d) whether it is fact that scarcity in LPG supply of this magnitude re-
surfaced on this occasion for the first time in the last seven years; and 
(e) the steps contemplated, if any, by Government to prevent its 
recurrence? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a), (d) and (e) Demand for LPG in the country is met by a 
combination of domestic production and imports. Atemporary shortage of LPG 
emerged in September 2005 when Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL), the single 
largest domestic supplier of LPG, announced a shut down of their Fluidized 
Catalytic Cracker (FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work with effect 
from October 2005, at just about th e time global LPG supplies became tight, 
domestic production was affected by the fire at Mumbai High and partly on 
account of the impact of Hurricane Katrina on US refineries. This upset the plans 
made by our Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) to effect imports in time to 
offset the anticipated shortage in supplies on account of the RIL shut down. 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2005] 
Further rumours in the market that OMCs would not be able to meet the 
demand led to a sudden spurt in demand. There was also a strike in bo ttling 
plants in the National Capital Territory (NCT) area towards the end of September, 
2005 which aggravated the situation. The Ministry took matters in hand early 
in October, 2005 when it was decided that through a combination of inventory 
management and imports, directly handled by a composite task force of the 
OMCs under the close supervision of the Government, physical shortages of 
supply would be overcome as quickly as possible. It was also decided that bottling 
plants in the NCT area would work on Sunday, 9th October 2005 and other 
holidays. On the basis of these decisions, it was announced that the physical 
shortage in the NCT area would end by Dusshera and substantively in the rest of 
the country by Deepavali. These objectives have been largely achieved. In 
addition to the arrangements made earlier by OMCs to import 642 Thousand 
Metric Tonnes (TMT) of LPG during the period October-December 2005, 
arrangements have been made to import an additional quantity of 237.9 TMT 
during this period, 116 TMT of which has already reached the country. Thus, the 
overall physical shortage in the country at present has been reduced to only 
about 1.5% of the average monthly consumption of LPG. However, the backlog 
at the micro-level may vary from market to market on account of operational 
reasons. The situation is expected to normalise further by the end of November, 
2005 on the restoration of production in RIL's refinery. Moreover, while OMCs 
are striving to ensure supplies to distributors in accordance with the registered 
customer strength of the distributor, the active cooperation of State Governments 
is required to cap, reduce and eventually eliminate the diversion of domestic LPG to 
the black market and unauthorized use which takes place on account of the wide 
gap between the retail price of LPG for domestic use and the market price for 
commercial LPG. The Union Government in the Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas has alerted State Governments to the imperative need to curtail 
diversion and other malpractices by enforcing the control orders issued under 
the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. OMCs have also been directed to ensure 
adherence to Marketing Discipline Guidelines, 2001. 
(b) OMCs market LPG in various parts of the country as per the 
requirements. The month-wise details of LPG sales during the period January 
2004-October 2005 is given in the enclosed Statement (See below). 
(c) During the period April-October 2005, OMCs have conducted 7461 
178 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
refill audits against their distributors for detecting diversion of domestic LPG 
cylinders. In these audits. 266 LPG distributors have been found to be involved 
in diversion. Penal action has been taken against all the erring distributors in 
accordance with the provisions of the Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG).

708. SHRI NANDIYELLAIAH: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:

180

Pradesh Government for additional allotment of 20,000 KL of kerosene per month

kerosene per month immediately, in the interest of additional BPL card-
holders; and

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKARAIYAR): (a) Yes, Sir.

Government/Union Territories, including the Government of Andhra Pradesh, for the

PDS kerosene has been allocated to States/UTs on a historical basis. In 
accordance with the policy adopted by the Government of India in 2000, kerosene

Availability of water in the country 
 †719. DR. MURLIMANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:      
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the availability of additional water in the country 
through rain and rivers is possible only for the very short period; 
(b) if not, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) if so, the estimate made for the time period in this regard; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that requirement of water in the country can be met only by 
way of storing water in the above situation; and 
(e) if so, Goverment's reation thereto and prospective scheme in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) to (c) About 75% of rainfall occurs 
during monsoon period (June to October) with a considerable part from a few spells of 
intense rainfall. 
(d) For meeting the requirement of water in the country, it is necessary to store and 
conserve the water. 
(e) Major, medium & minor water resources schemes are planned by the respective 
State Governments for meeting the requirements. Further measures like rainwater 
harvesting and ground water recharge are also adopted for conserving the water.

Improvement in quality of drinking water 
722. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that inspite of sincere efforts by the Central 
Government, the States have not improved the quality of drinking water; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether guidelines issued by Government to States for routine 
analysis of samples for physio-chemicals and microbial quality are not being 
followed by States; and 
(d) if so, the remedial steps being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) No, Sir, 96.13% of the. 
14,22,303 rural habitations in the country have been fully covered, and 3.55% 
partially covered with safe drinking water supply as per the stipulated norms. 
(b) Due to overexploitation of groundwater and other factors, some of the 
drinking water sources become chemically contaminated and unsafe. The number 
of water quality affected habitations in the country as on 31.3.2004, as reported 
by State Governments in response to water quality survey ordered in March, 
2000 is 2,16,968. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. The quality of drinking water of various sources is 
periodically monitored by the District Water Quality Testing Laboratories set 
up by States and other available labora tories with reference to the water 
quality standards laid down by the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water 
Mission (RGNDWM) as per IS:10500 standard. A community based rural drinking 
water monitoring and surveillance programme has also been pilot-tested in four 
districts of the country for scaling up throughout the country.

nation-wide campaign to raise ground water level, by way of conventional

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF  THE MINISTRY OF WATER

(i) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground

(ii) Launching of a website on Roof  Top Rain Water Harvesting Error! 
Hyperlink reference not valid. to make aware and educate the public 
about various techniques of harvesting rainwater and store it for future

(iii) Organisation of mass awareness programmes and training courses on 
rainwater harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. 
(iv) Rain Water Harvesting campaign has been launched keeping in view 
the various target groups like youth and children, women, farmers and 
villagers, policy and opinion makers. Publicity through print media, 
telecasting of spots on the television, broadcasting messages on radio, 
holding of seminars, workshops, conferences etc., have been 
undertaken for the purpose. 
(v) All the States/UTs have been requested to provide water harvesting

National Highways Authority of India have been requested to provide

of India have amended Building Bye-laws, 1983, making provision for water 
harvesting through storing of water run-off including rain water in all new

State Governments of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, 
Rajasthan and Kerala have made roof top rain water harvesting mandatory in

water harvesting structures.

a Pilot scheme on "National Project for Repair, Renovation and Restoration of Water

Revamping of Water Management 
725. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Bank has in a recen t report portrayed a very dismal 
picture of the future of water resources and water management in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to revamp the water management in the 
country so that India does not face water famine as apprehended in the World 
Bank report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) and (b) Mr. John 
Briscoe of the World Bank has recently prepared a draft Report titled "India's 
Water Economy: Bracing for a Turbulent Future". The report is based on 
study conducted by the World Bank on its own. The report in 
206 

[29 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
general discusses various aspects of water resources development and 
management in India and broadly covers the issues related to; 
(i) adjusting to the needs of a changing India; 
(ii) adjusting to scarcity and greater variability; 
(iii) dealing with growing conflicts; 
(iv) maintaining and renewing existing infrastructure; 
(v)    building infrastructure in under-served areas and for under served public 
puposes; 
(vi)    making the transition from development to management and 
development; 
(vii)    revitalizing the machinery of government to deal with the turbulent water 
future; and 
(viii)    charting a prioritized, sequenced, pragmatic path for making 
improvements. 
Most of issues are duly addressed in the National Water Policy and 
appropriate actions are taken in light of the present policies of the Union and 
State Governments. 
(c) The National Water Policy, 2002 clearly states that drought prone areas 
should be made less vulnerable to drought associated problems through soil-
moisture conservation measures, water harvesting practices, minimization of 
evaporation losses, development of the ground water potential including 
recharging and the transfer of surface water from surplus areas where feasible and 
appropriate and pastures, forestry or other modes of development which are 
relatively less water demanding should be encouraged. The National Water 
Policy further states that in planning water resource development projects, the 
needs of drought prone areas should be given priority.

adoption of traditional techniques like mulching or pitcher irrigation and new 
techniques like drip and sprinkler may be promoted, wherever feasible.

MOTION 
 Condemnation of alleged involvement of Indian entities and individuals as 
non-contractual beneficiaries of United Nations' Oil-for-Food-Programme in 
Iraq as reported by Volcker Committee 
SHRI ARUN JAITLEY (Gujarat): Mr. Chairman, Sir, let me first express my 
gratitude to you for permitting me to move this Motion under rule 167. The Motion 
I move reads: 
"That this House strongly condemns t he alleged involvement of some Indian 
entities and individuals as non-contractual beneficiaries of the United 
Nations' Oil-for-Food-Programme in Iraq, as reported in the Report of the 
United Nations' Independent Inquiry Committee (Volcker Committee)." 
Sir, in the past few weeks, we have had from the Government at the highest 
level and from the political parties whose alliance and coalition is in power certain 
responses to what has been stated in the Independent Inquiry Committee's 
Report. Let us remember, and this needs to be underlined, that this Report is 
no ordinary document. This Report has not only domestic significance, as far as 
India is concerned, this Report is a document of high international credibility. And 
amongst others, this Report has mentioned, at least, two prominent Indian 
entities along with a third one, then, there are several other companies, and what 
has disturbed the country the most is a reference to a political party which has been 
in power in India for the longest duration of time as also a very hon. Member of this
